# The Most Recently Described Genus of Colosteidae as of August 1, 2024

## Executive Summary
Based on available research data, Deltaherpeton represents the most recently formally described genus of Colosteidae, established through the description of Deltaherpeton hiemstrae in 2010 from the Mississippian of Iowa. Colosteidae is an extinct family of stem-group tetrapods (stegocephalians) that lived during the Carboniferous period, spanning from the Viséan to the late Moscovian stages. The family currently contains four recognized genera: Colosteus (the type genus), Deltaherpeton, Greererpeton, and Pholidogaster, with no new genera reported in the 2024 scientific literature as of the research cutoff date.

Deltaherpeton hiemstrae was described by Berman and colleagues and published in the Journal of Paleontology in 2010. This discovery and formal description predates the August 1, 2024 research query date by approximately 14 years, making it the most recently described genus within Colosteidae available in the current research dataset. No evidence of subsequent genus descriptions within Colosteidae between 2010 and August 2024 was identified in the approved research claims or available databases.

## Key Findings
- Deltaherpeton is the most recently described genus of Colosteidae, formally established through the 2010 publication of Deltaherpeton hiemstrae in the Journal of Paleontology (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-paleontology/article/deltaherpeton-hiemstrae-a-new-colosteid-tetrapod-from-the-mississippian-of-iowa/700D38417E0886EDD7F60906B3137C8D)
- Colosteidae contains exactly four recognized genera: Colosteus (type genus), Deltaherpeton, Greererpeton, and Pholidogaster (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosteidae, https://fossil.fandom.com/wiki/Colosteidae)
- Deltaherpeton hiemstrae was discovered in Mississippian-age deposits of Iowa, representing the most recent formal genus and species description within the family (https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010JPal...84.1135B/abstract)
- Colosteidae was established as a family by Cope in 1875 and comprises stem-group tetrapods that lived during the Carboniferous period, specifically from the Viséan to late Moscovian stages (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosteidae)
- No new Colosteidae genera were reported in 2024 based on major species announcement databases and the Catalogue of Life 2024 annual release (https://explorersweb.com/190-new-species-discovered-in-2024, https://www.catalogueoflife.org/2024/06/27/annual-release)
- Colosteids possessed distinctive anatomical features including approximately 40 vertebrae excluding the tail, characteristic of stem-tetrapod morphology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosteidae)

## Deltaherpeton: The Most Recently Described Genus
Deltaherpeton represents the most recently formally described genus within Colosteidae as of August 1, 2024. The type species, Deltaherpeton hiemstrae, was formally described in 2010 in the Journal of Paleontology through work by Berman and colleagues. The specimen was recovered from Mississippian-age deposits in Iowa, representing a significant discovery for understanding early tetrapod evolution. The genus name reflects its phylogenetic position and morphological characteristics within the colosteid radiation. The formal description of Deltaherpeton hiemstrae provided new insights into colosteid diversity and paleobiogeography during the early Carboniferous period (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-paleontology/article/deltaherpeton-hiemstrae-a-new-colosteid-tetrapod-from-the-mississippian-of-iowa/700D38417E0886EDD7F60906B3137C8D; https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2010JPal...84.1135B/abstract).

## Colosteidae Family Composition and Taxonomy
Colosteidae is recognized as a well-defined family within the larger clade of stegocephalians (stem-group tetrapods). The family was formally established by Cope in 1875 and currently comprises four genera: Colosteus, Deltaherpeton, Greererpeton, and Pholidogaster. Colosteus serves as the type genus for the family, establishing the nomenclatural foundation for Colosteidae. Each genus represents a distinct lineage within the family, though their specific phylogenetic relationships continue to be refined through comparative anatomical and cladistic analyses. The four-genus composition of Colosteidae has remained stable in recent taxonomic treatments, with no additional genera described since Deltaherpeton's establishment in 2010 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosteidae; https://fossil.fandom.com/wiki/Colosteidae).

## Temporal and Phylogenetic Context
Colosteidae inhabited aquatic and semi-aquatic environments during a specific interval of the Carboniferous period, ranging from the Viséan stage through the late Moscovian stage. This temporal distribution spans a significant portion of the early to middle Carboniferous, representing approximately 30 million years of paleobiogeographic presence. As stem-group tetrapods, colosteids occupied a crucial phylogenetic position in the early radiation of tetrapods, preceding the diversification of crown-group Tetrapoda. The family exhibits morphological features characteristic of early tetrapods, including the aforementioned complement of approximately 40 vertebrae (excluding the tail), aquatic adaptations, and intermediate characteristics between fish-like ancestors and more derived tetrapods. Their geographical distribution included at least North America, though additional localities may reflect incomplete fossil records (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosteidae; https://fossil.fandom.com/wiki/Colosteidae).

## Research Status and Knowledge Gaps as of August 2024
As of August 1, 2024, no new colosteid genera have been described in the paleontological literature since Deltaherpeton's establishment in 2010. This 14-year interval without new genus-level descriptions suggests that either colosteid diversity has been adequately characterized from available fossil material, or such material remains undiscovered or undescribed in collections. Major species announcement databases and the Catalogue of Life's 2024 annual release contain no records of newly described Colosteidae genera, indicating that active research on this family has not yielded novel higher-level taxonomic discoveries in recent years. However, ongoing work on existing specimens may continue to refine understanding of colosteid morphology, phylogenetics, and paleobiology without necessarily adding new genera to the family (https://explorersweb.com/190-new-species-discovered-in-2024; https://www.catalogueoflife.org/2024/06/27/annual-release).

## Confidence Assessment
Moderate to High confidence. The claim that Deltaherpeton is the most recently described genus of Colosteidae rests on multiple converging lines of evidence: (1) explicit documentation of Deltaherpeton hiemstrae's 2010 description in the Journal of Paleontology with high-quality peer-reviewed sources; (2) consistent reporting across multiple authoritative sources (Wikipedia, Fossil Fandom, Cambridge University Press) that Colosteidae contains four genera with Deltaherpeton among them; (3) negative evidence from 2024 species databases showing no new Colosteidae genera reported this year. The primary limitations are the relatively narrow temporal window of the research query (only through August 1, 2024) and the moderate coverage score (0.45), which suggests the available research dataset may not have achieved exhaustive coverage of all paleontological literature. The source diversity score of 0.58 indicates reasonable but not comprehensive source representation.

## Limitations
This report is subject to several important limitations: (1) The research cutoff date of August 1, 2024 means that any genera described between this date and the present are not captured; (2) The coverage score of 0.45 indicates that approximately 55% of potentially relevant information may not be included in the dataset, particularly specialized paleontological monographs or regional publications not indexed in major databases; (3) The absence of evidence for new descriptions is not definitive proof that none exist—discovery of new material in museum collections or specialized journals outside the searched databases remains possible; (4) This analysis depends on the accuracy and completeness of the 'Catalogue of Life' 2024 release and Explorersweb's species announcement database, both of which may have incomplete coverage of paleontological literature; (5) The temporal scope for identifying 'recently described' is constrained by the query date, and changing this reference point would necessarily alter which genus is identified as most recent; (6) No access to comprehensive paleontological journals beyond the sources cited was available, potentially missing relevant publications in specialized or regional journals.
